title: Township transit funding bid and brownfield tax grants
subtitle: Winter maintenance debrief, recycling transition reporting, and requested staff follow-ups on sidewalks, conservation authority changes and a Cambridge bus loop.
overview: The Sustainability, Infrastructure, and Development Committee recommended that the Region endorse Grand River Transit's application to the Ontario Transit Investment Fund for new and expanded Township transit {{vote:m1}}. The plan starts in fall 2026 with new fixed routes and on-demand service in North Dumfries and Wellesley, plus expanded service in Wilmot and Woolwich, and later extends on-demand service to all townships.

The committee also recommended two joint Tax Increment Grants for redeveloped, previously contaminated downtown Kitchener sites: 120 Victoria Street South, capped at $656,291 {{vote:m2}}, and 108 Garment Street, capped at $745,641 {{vote:m3}}. Staff said recent provincial changes allow the Region to offer these grants again. The grants are paid from new tax revenue after redevelopment.

It recommended that staff work with Circular Materials on shared curbside recycling information and report in early 2027 on landfill volumes and resident inquiries {{vote:m4}}. The committee received a winter maintenance report for information. Staff were asked to look at sidewalk and bus stop clearing costs, and to report on proposed conservation authority changes.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended endorsing Grand River Transit's Ontario Transit Investment Fund application for new and improved Township transit services.

decisions.item: Tax Increment Grant, 120 Victoria Street South
decisions.detail: The committee recommended a joint Tax Increment Grant, with the Regional amount capped at $656,291 and financed from incremental tax revenue, and authorized staff to sign related agreements.
The committee recommended a joint Tax Increment Grant, with the Regional amount capped at $745,641 and financed from incremental tax revenue, and authorized staff to sign related agreements.
The committee recommended that staff share Circular Materials' curbside collection information where possible and report in Q1 2027 on landfill volumes and resident inquiries after the transition.

debate: On the transit application, one councillor asked whether Township on-demand service would be faster than the current Mobility Plus model, which needs about three hours' notice. Staff said the aim is as on-demand as possible, possibly including same-day pickup, depending on vehicle availability.

Councillors asked what happens if ridership falls short. Staff said provincial funding is meant to taper over five years, and that any decision to continue or change service would be made with the townships. Staff expected the province to allow service changes, and one councillor stressed the need for that flexibility.

On winter maintenance, councillors raised snowbanks left by plows at bus stops and crosswalks as barriers for people with mobility needs. Staff said bus stop clearing starts after 48 hours, that costing faster clearing would be part of the area maintenance agreement work, and that clearing sidewalks first could mean moving snow twice and runs against provincial minimum standards.

On the Tax Increment Grants, one councillor asked how they work. Staff said the grants rebate new tax revenue to the developer after remediation, redevelopment and reassessment, rather than waiving taxes. Another councillor asked why the Brownfield program ended. Staff said its development charge exemption was costly, while the grants fund themselves from the tax base.

On recycling, the mover was concerned that less frequent collection could push more material to landfill and generate resident calls. Councillors urged a shared 2026 collection calendar with Circular Materials, but staff said timing was tight. The mover hoped for a cost-shared calendar in 2027.
